THE STATUTORY FAIR USE DEFENSE AND ITS ILLUSTRATIVE LIST OF PURPOSES
Federal copyright law creates a fair use defense in a single statutory provision. Under 17 U.S.C. § 107, "[n]otwithstanding the provisions of sections 106 and 106A, the fair use of a copyrighted work, including such use by reproduction in copies or phonorecords or by any other means specified by that section, for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), scholarship, or research, is not an infringement of copyright." The specific purposes named in that sentence -- criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research -- are introduced with the words "such as," and the Copyright Act's own definitions section states that "[t]he terms 'including' and 'such as' are illustrative and not limitative." 17 U.S.C. § 101. A use is accordingly not disqualified from fair use merely because it serves some purpose other than the six purposes § 107 happens to name, and a use is not automatically fair use merely because it does match one of them; the named purposes are examples of the kind of use fair use can cover, not a closed list. The work identified in this document, a photograph published in 2020, and the use described as a critical commentary blog post quoting a short excerpt, are addressed by the remaining clauses in this document, which describe the four-factor analysis § 107 requires in every case.

THE FOUR STATUTORY FACTORS
The fair use statute does not leave the analysis to open-ended judicial discretion; it names four factors that a court must consider. Under 17 U.S.C. § 107, "[i]n determining whether the use made of a work in any particular case is a fair use the factors to be considered shall include -- (1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes; (2) the nature of the copyrighted work; (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole; and (4) the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work." The statute also adds a rule specific to unpublished works: "[t]he fact that a work is unpublished shall not itself bar a finding of fair use if such finding is made upon consideration of all the above factors." As with the illustrative list of purposes in this provision's opening sentence, the phrase "shall include" before the four factors is not read as a closed list -- 17 U.S.C. § 101 states that "the terms 'including' and 'such as' are illustrative and not limitative" -- so a court may weigh considerations beyond the four named factors, though the four are the ones the statute specifically requires to be considered in every case.

"TRANSFORMATIVE USE" IS A JUDICIAL GLOSS ON FACTOR ONE, NOT STATUTORY TEXT
The word "transformative" does not appear anywhere in 17 U.S.C. § 107. It is a term courts use when applying the statute's first factor -- the purpose and character of the use -- and its leading source is the Supreme Court's 1994 decision in Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994), a case about whether a commercial rap-music parody of a rock ballad could be a fair use. Explaining what the first factor asks, the Court wrote that a court must consider whether the new work "adds something new, with a further purpose or different character, altering the first with new expression, meaning, or message; it asks, in other words, whether and to what extent the new work is 'transformative.'" The Court also made clear that this judge-made concept is not a mandatory checkbox: "[a]lthough such transformative use is not absolutely necessary for a finding of fair use," the Court explained, a more transformative use makes the other statutory factors, including commercial character, matter less to the outcome. A use can accordingly be evaluated for how transformative it is under the first statutory factor, but "transformative use" itself is case law's label for part of that factor's analysis, not separate statutory language, and satisfying or failing it does not by itself decide fair use.

NO FIXED PERCENTAGE, WORD COUNT, OR BRIGHT-LINE RULE
Neither the fair use statute nor the case law applying it sets a specific percentage, word count, or other numeric threshold that automatically makes a use fair or unfair. The statute's third factor asks about "the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole," 17 U.S.C. § 107(3), without specifying any number, proportion, or length. On the amount-used factor specifically, the Court explained that "the extent of permissible copying varies with the purpose and character of the use" -- meaning the same amount of copying can be reasonable for one purpose and excessive for another, so no fixed quantity is inherently safe or inherently disqualifying.

FAIR USE AS AN AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE, AND WHO CARRIES THE BURDEN
Section 107 itself does not say who has the burden of proving fair use -- it states that a qualifying use "is not an infringement of copyright" and lists the factors a court considers, without allocating a burden of proof to either side. Consistent with that description, fair use is examined by weighing all four statutory factors together in light of the facts of a particular use, rather than by treating any single factor, or any use that happens to resemble one of § 107's listed purposes, as automatically establishing or defeating the defense.
